title: US Locks In $4B Polish Military Financing as Pentagon Scouts New Bases; Directed-Energy Counter-Drone Enters Production
subhead: Washington signed a sixth Foreign Military Financing guarantee with Poland worth $4 billion — pushing total US defense support toward $20 billion — while a US delegation including top strategist Elbridge Colby toured potential new permanent base sites. Separately, the US Army's first production contract for a high-energy laser weapon and AeroVironment's first foreign LOCUST order mark directed energy's shift from prototype to routine procurement.

sections.heading: Poland Deepens US Ties: $4B Loan Guarantee Plus Base Site Scouting
sections.body:
Washington and Warsaw signed a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee on September 9, Poland's sixth under the program, according to Stars and Stripes and the State Department. The State Department said the deal brings total US defense support to Poland to nearly $20 billion. The guarantee is aimed at accelerating Poland's existing $10 billion purchase of 96 AH-64E Apache helicopters.

Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said at the signing that Poland 'is taking greater responsibility for the security of Europe,' calling the country 'an absolute leader' in defense spending. The Stripes report notes Poland dedicates roughly 4.5% of GDP to its military. The financing coincided with a US delegation visiting Poland on Thursday and Friday to inspect potential locations for permanent American bases, with Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Bejda telling TVP that Elbridge Colby, a senior Pentagon strategist, was part of the tour. Warsaw has pledged to fund a new base that could cost about $3 billion, Bejda said.
sections.whyItMatters: This locks Poland in as the centerpiece of a US force-posture shift toward the eastern flank. With the Pentagon reviewing its European base footprint and Poland hosting a rare permanent US base in Poznan, the loan guarantee and base talks signal Warsaw is positioning itself as the primary hub for relocated American forces, not just a large buyer of hardware.

sections.heading: Directed Energy Crosses the Line: Army's First Laser Production Contract and LOCUST's First Export
sections.body:
US directed-energy counter-drone capability moved from experimentation into sustained procurement this week. On September 2 the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million agreement for the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program — described by the service as its first production contract for a high-energy laser weapon, Army Recognition reports. Days later, on September 8, AeroVironment announced a first international purchase order for its LOCUST laser weapon system worth more than $50 million to an undisclosed foreign customer, a direct commercial sale.

The 30-kilowatt LOCUST X3, rated for engagements under $10 per shot, has an unusual operational record for a newly exported laser: Army Recognition notes acknowledged kills against drones during US southern-border operations and successful tests from the flight deck of the carrier USS George H.W. Bush. AeroVironment is expanding LOCUST manufacturing in Albuquerque, New Mexico, with more than $30 million in announced investment tied to the Army program.
sections.whyItMatters: Two milestones landing within six days — the Army's first production buy and a foreign sale — take directed energy past the demonstration phase. The strategic point is economic: lasers can absorb repeated drone attacks at marginal cost, letting militaries conserve finite, expensive interceptors, a lesson driven home by drone warfare in Ukraine, the Middle East and the Red Sea.

sections.heading: Pentagon Tests Whether Lasers Can Work as Routine Base Defense
sections.body:
The Pentagon's Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF 401) has launched a yearlong operational assessment of directed-energy counter-drone systems across multiple US military installations, according to an Army Recognition analysis of a September 9 Department of War statement. Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, JIATF 401 director, said the task force intends to keep lasers and high-power microwave systems on bases for 365 days, with military personnel responsible for operating and maintaining them — shifting focus from demonstration to endurance, mission-capability rates, power demand, cooling and airspace deconfliction.

The pilot builds on the five installations selected in May 2026 and folds in systems like the 20-kilowatt-class AMP-HEL and the 50-kilowatt DE M-SHORAD on a Stryker. JIATF 401 is also planning a directed-energy shoot-off in December with the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, with technologies that meet performance requirements potentially moving toward purchase orders.
sections.whyItMatters: The question being tested is whether directed energy can become a repeatable base-defense model rather than a set-piece demonstration. The results will inform whether the US — and by extension NATO allies — treat lasers and microwaves as a sustainable layer of counter-UAS architecture, influencing allied procurement while pushing adversaries toward larger salvos and hardened electronics.

sections.heading: Russia Markets Su-57E and Hybrid Drone-Missiles at El Alamein Airshow
sections.body:
Russia's state arms exporter Rosoboronexport used the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt (September 8-10) to debut its export Su-57E fifth-generation fighter at an African airshow and publicly display the S-71M and S-71K, systems the Defense Watch describes as blurring the line between cruise missiles and attack drones, per Reuters reporting. Reuters noted military delegations from Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Kuwait attended. Russia's display paired the fighter with air-launched unmanned strike systems, pitching an integrated crewed-uncrewed package rather than a standalone aircraft.

Rostec said the S-71 family features low observability, long range and high speed, but The Defense Watch flags that detailed specifications such as range, payload and guidance have not been publicly released. The outlet notes the Su-57E had previously appeared at shows in China, India and the UAE, and arrives on the export market with operational visibility from combat use in Ukraine.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is betting export buyers want a crewed-uncrewed package — a fifth-generation fighter paired with lower-cost strike drones — reflecting lessons from the war in Ukraine about mass and cost. But without released performance data, and with production capacity and sanctions constraints, the pitch is more ambition than proven capability, contested by Chinese, Turkish and Gulf suppliers also present at the show.

sections.heading: Turkey and Egypt Move Co-Produced Hamza-1 Drone to Commercial Sales
sections.body:
Turkish firm Havelsan and Egypt's state Arab Organization for Industrialization (AOI) signed a commercial agreement at the El Alamein Airshow to begin sales of their jointly developed Hamza-1 UAV, according to Anadolu Agency as reported by Middle East Monitor. The deal follows a cooperation agreement signed in August 2025 to build vertical takeoff and landing drones in Egypt, combining Havelsan's autonomous-systems engineering with AOI's local manufacturing.

The prototype of the Hamza-1 was first unveiled at the EDEX defense expo in Cairo late last year. Middle East Monitor notes the deal highlights growing defense-industrial cooperation between Ankara and Cairo, and Havelsan's broader global co-production strategy built on its Baha, Bozbey, Poyraz and Bulut domestic drone platforms.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is deepening a defense-industrial relationship with Egypt at a time the two countries are normalizing ties, and co-production is the political vehicle — local jobs and technology transfer make the relationship stickier than a simple arms sale. It also shows Turkish drone and autonomous-systems expertise moving from export sales into joint manufacturing partnerships.

sections.heading: China's HQ-17AE Shorad Systems Head to Pakistan as Drone Threat Grows
sections.body:
Pakistan is fielding Chinese HQ-17AE short-range air defense systems, a platform designed partly to counter small drones, at a time of persistent tensions with India, according to a report by The Star citing analysts. The development follows Pakistan displaying air-defense systems resembling China's HQ-17A. The Star quoted an analyst saying successful integration of the HQ-17AE with other foreign systems in Pakistani service would strengthen China's export case 'considerably'.

The system is positioned to bolster Pakistan's protection against drones and short-range aerial threats as drone swarm attacks become a more common feature of regional conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: This is part of China's push to sell capable, affordable air defense to the Global South and South Asia, where drone threats are proliferating. For Islamabad it fills a short-range air defense gap against cheap drones without relying on expensive Western interceptors — and for Beijing, Pakistan serves as a validation and marketing case for the HQ-17AE family.

bottomLine: US-Polish defense deepening was the day's anchor: a $4 billion loan guarantee, nearly $20 billion in cumulative US support, and Pentagon strategist Elbridge Colby touring candidate sites for new permanent American bases. Around it, the defense industry's center of gravity moved on directed energy — the Army's first laser production contract, LOCUST's first export, and a yearlong Pentagon base-defense trial — marking a concrete shift from prototype demonstrations toward repeatable procurement. Russia and Turkey both used the El Alamein airshow to court buyers with crewed-uncrewed strike packages and co-production deals, while China's air-defense exports to Pakistan extended its reach into South Asia. The through-line: affordability and reusability against drone swarms are now driving procurement decisions across the West, Russia's export strategy, and the Global South alike.
sources: Stars and Stripes, US State Department, Army Recognition, Defense Watch, Reuters, Middle East Monitor, Anadolu Agency, The Star, JIATF 401/Department of War statement, AeroVironment
